🧠 Crypto News Brief: Soft US jobs data and fading Fed-hike bets lifted Bitcoin toward $87K, while regulators in Washington and Brussels advanced crypto rulebooks and institutions from Tokyo to Tether pushed deeper into on-chain finance. 📊 Weak US Jobs Report Lifts Bitcoin Toward $87K The US added just 29,000 jobs in September, far below the roughly 90,000 economists expected, while unemployment ticked up to 4.2% and August was revised down to 133,000. Bitcoin held its gains and traded just under $87,000 as markets slashed the odds of an October Fed hike to about 13%. Derivatives traders had already piled in: open interest climbed by roughly $2.3 billion since Sept. 30, and perpetual funding rates rose from about 3% to 10%. Read full story → 🏛️ SEC Proposes Crypto Custody Rules as Peirce Exits The Securities and Exchange Commission proposed a dedicated custody framework for registered investment advisers and regulated funds holding crypto. Advisers could act as custodians themselves in limited cases, such as when no permitted custodian exists for an asset, and state-chartered trust companies would qualify as custodians. Chair Paul Atkins said the plan creates a compliant pathway where none existed. A 60-day comment period opens after Federal Register publication. The proposal lands as Commissioner Hester Peirce, architect of the Crypto Task Force, departs on Friday, leaving the SEC with only two commissioners. More details → 🇸🇻 IMF Waives El Salvador's Bitcoin Breach, Releases $139M The IMF board completed the second and third reviews of El Salvador's $1.4 billion loan program and released roughly $139 million, granting a waiver even though the country breached its limit on Bitcoin accumulation. The Fund accepted documentation that the extra coins came from private donations rather than public money, but said no further accumulation is envisaged beyond documented gifts. The program also requires a smaller state role in the Chivo wallet, now majority-controlled by a private operator. Read more → 💵 Tether's USDT Is Coming Home to Bitcoin Tether's USDT, which first launched on Bitcoin's Omni Layer in 2014 before migrating to Ethereum and Tron, is set to return to Bitcoin this month. Tether-backed Utexo, which holds a commercial license to issue the token on Bitcoin, will use the RGB protocol to enable private USDT transfers, direct BTC-USDT swaps

80125.subject: What is this century’s biggest idea?
80125.body:
The Economist Picks

Автор: The Economist


Автор: The Economist

    
    
    Прочитайте цю статтю на LinkedIn, щоб приєднатися до обговорення
Прочитати на LinkedIn
https://www.linkedin.com/comm/pulse/what-centurys-biggest-idea-the-economist-eqsge?lipi=urn%3Ali%3Apage%3Aemail_email_series_follow_newsletter_02%3Ba8caMkiRQSOTrMueUs5SuQ%3D%3D&midToken=AQFTjFOONAfT2w&midSig=23tGcjA_-Ltss1&trk=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_&trkEmail=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_-null-fz96fz~muqvbsys~mx-null-null&eid=fz96fz-muqvbsys-mx
  
Enjoying this newsletter? Get it in your inbox every Thursday, as well as our bonus weekend round-up of The Economist’s best journalism, by signing up for free here. When I was a student I sold Christmas cards to raise money for UNICEF. To potential donors sipping ale in English pubs, I’d stress that for less than the price of a pint they could pay for a vaccine shot that might save the life of a child in Africa. Many reached for their wallets, but I remember one who said, in a rather peeved voice: “Why don’t you raise money for British children?” It is a fair question. I was taking a hyper-rational approach to charity: the same donation can relieve far more suffering in a poor country than in a rich one. But many people feel more empathy for those closer by. In “Bleak House” Charles Dickens mocked a character called Mrs Jellyby, who was obsessed with helping the inhabitants of Borrioboola-Gha, a fictional sub-Saharan locale, while neglecting her own home and children. I wonder what Dickens—let alone the man in that pub—would have made of the “effective altruists” (EAs) who now dominate Silicon Valley. As we report this week, their philosophy is the biggest idea of this century so far. And it takes the Mrs Jellyby principle to extremes. Not only do far-away people have the same claim on our goodwill as those standing next to us. Many EAs think we should care—a lot—about the billions or trillions of people who may be born in the distant future. Some also think that, because animals can suffer, we should worry as much about prawns as we do about people. Our cover package explores these ideas. Only a few people are EAs, but they are hugely influential, since they staff the most advanced artificial-intelligence companies. Some of their insights are sound. It really is better if charity is cost-effective, and we really should take seriously the possibility that AI could go rogue and do immense harm. But sometimes their logic leads them to odd places. If your moral calculations depend on predicting what the world will be like in the year 2300, there is a good chance they will be hooey. And if you are both powerful and utterly convinced you know what’s best for humanity—well, that combination didn’t work out so well during some of the high-minded revolutions of the past, from France’s in 1789 to Russia’s in 1917. Crypto companies are raising billions again, but investors are no longer handing out premiums indiscriminately. Kalshi is reportedly seeking $1 billion at a $40 billion valuation, nearly twice what it was worth in May. Meanwhile, Blockchain.com is preparing for an initial public offering (IPO) at a potential $6 billion valuation, well below the $14 billion it commanded during the last crypto boom. The divide is even sharper among digital asset treasury companies, where just four of the 20 largest still trade above the value of their crypto holdings. This week’s Crypto Biz looks at where investors are still willing to pay up, where the old crypto premium has disappeared and how Bitget is dealing with the fallout from a $388 million security breach. Only 4 of top 20 crypto treasury companies still trade above NAV: DWF The crypto treasury model has largely lost its early advantage, with most digital asset treasury (DAT) companies no longer commanding the premiums that once helped them raise capital and accumulate crypto without diluting shareholders, according to DWF Ventures. DWF’s report found only four of the 20 largest DATs by assets under management trade above an mNAV of 1: Bit Digital, Strive, Hyperliquid Strategies and BitMine. The discounts suggest investors are no longer willing to pay the same premium for crypto exposure through public companies. Since Michael Saylor’s Strategy pioneered the Bitcoin treasury model in 2020, most DAT stocks have underperformed simply holding the underlying crypto asset. That premium allows companies to issue shares and buy more crypto without diluting existing holders. When shares trade below NAV, however, raising equity can become dilutive and undermine the model’s core financing mechanism.
